This is for mutation testing, the software testing technique that measures how well a project's own test suite detects small deliberate changes to its code. Each changed copy is run only against that project's tests in an isolated checkout and is then discarded; nothing is deployed or executed elsewhere. The tool that makes the changes is called the mutation engine.

The mutation engine reads one small JSON data pack per programming language. The engine itself knows no language. It parses source files with the tree-sitter grammar that ast-grep ships for the language, finds syntax nodes the pack names, and rewrites them with the templates the pack gives. You write the pack for one language. You are given packs for other languages as examples of the format, not as content to copy: node kind names differ between grammars.

## Fields

Every node kind named anywhere in the pack must be an exact node type of the target language's grammar; one unknown kind makes the whole pack invalid. Confirm each name against that grammar only. Do not infer a kind from the meaning of a construct, from another language, or from an example pack: the examples show the JSON shape, never the node vocabulary. When a construct may have several grammar spellings, include only the spellings you have verified. If you are unsure, omit the entry or leave the optional list empty; a smaller pack with only certain kinds is safer than a broad pack with guessed kinds. The same strictness applies to field names, operator tokens, attribute kinds, and prefix text.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `language` | The language name as ast-grep spells it, lower case |
| `comment_kinds` | Node kinds of comments. Nothing inside them is ever touched. Include only comment forms the target grammar actually has |
| `string_kinds` | Node kinds of string literals, including multi-part or template strings. Nothing inside them is ever touched. If the grammar has several literal spellings, list only the ones you can confirm; do not guess extra variants |
| `unwrap_kinds` | Node kinds of a grouping wrapper that belongs to a statement's syntax around a condition. When a condition is such a wrapper, the engine works on the expression inside it. Empty when conditions are not wrapped |
| `test_attribute_markers` | Text fragments of attributes or annotations that mark test-only code inside a production file. Empty when the language keeps tests in separate files. Match each fragment exactly as written, and include separate fragments for outer and inner attribute forms when the language has both |
| `test_attribute_kinds` | Node kinds of the attribute or annotation items that can stand directly in front of a declaration and carry one of the `test_attribute_markers`. Required when `test_attribute_markers` is not empty; leave it out otherwise. If inner attributes can mark an entire file, module, or block as test-only, list their node kind here too, not only the kind that sits before a single declaration |
| `kinds.branch_condition.field_of` | Pairs `[statement kind, field name]`: the named field of that statement kind holds a condition that decides control flow. List the conditional and loop statements and conditional expressions whose grammar rule has such a field |
| `kinds.branch_condition.returned` | `{"of", "kinds", "tokens"}`: `of` lists the node kinds of a return; `kinds` the node kinds of logical, comparison and negation expressions; `tokens` the operator tokens that make such an expression a yes-or-no value. A returned expression of one of these kinds with one of these operators is a condition. Use only operator tokens that exist in the target language |
| `kinds.failure_state.nodes` | Node kinds that signal failure to the caller: raising or throwing, returning, propagating an error. A listed non-return kind must be actionable through the failure operators; returns are handled through returned-literal swaps, so do not give them a general replacement template |
| `kinds.failure_state.nodes_with_prefix` | Optional. Node kind mapped to text prefixes, for failure signals that are ordinary calls or macros in this language and can only be told apart by how they begin. Use this for call-shaped failure signals too, not only for macro punctuation; choose the node kind that really represents an ordinary call expression in the target grammar and spell each prefix exactly as it begins in the source |
| `kinds.error_order.nodes` | The node kind of a conditional statement that can directly follow another one of the same kind. Always with `"requires_next_sibling": true` |
| `kinds.state_write.nodes` | Node kinds of assignments and in-place updates. If compound or updated assignment is the same node kind as assignment with an operator token, list that assignment kind once; do not invent a separate kind |
| `kinds.state_write.call_statements` | Node kinds of a call, and of an awaited call where the language has one, that can stand alone as a statement. Such a statement counts as a write made through a call. Use the grammar's real distinction between plain calls and method calls; do not copy that distinction from another language |
| `kinds.pure_shell_boundary.nodes` | Node kinds of function and method definitions |
| `noop_statement` | Text of a statement that does nothing and is valid wherever a statement may stand |
| `statement_wrappers` | Node kinds that wrap an expression to make it a statement of its own |
| `statement_terminator` | The token that ends a simple statement, if the language has one; leave it out otherwise |

## Operators

An operator entry must line up with a site listed under `kinds`. Do not define an operator for a node kind that is not listed where that site belongs, and do not list a rewritable site without giving the engine a way to rewrite it.

| Entry | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `operators.branch_condition.template` | Replaces a condition by its logical negation. The result must be valid syntax in the place where the condition stood, for any condition expression. If the language needs grouping around a negated expression in some positions, the template itself must include that grouping |
| `operators.branch_condition.token_swaps` | Pairs of operator tokens that can replace each other without changing the type of the expression: equal and not equal, a strict and a non-strict comparison, logical and and or. Spell them exactly as the language does |
| `operators.branch_condition.negation_swaps` | The pairs among `token_swaps` whose swap gives exactly the logical negation of the comparison: equal and not equal, in every spelling the language has. The engine uses it to avoid producing the same change twice. Do not list a strict and a non-strict comparison, or and and or |
| `operators.branch_condition.exclude_kinds` | Optional. Node kinds that can appear in a condition position but cannot be negated by the template, such as a pattern-binding condition or an empty condition. Only list names you can confirm in the target grammar |
| `operators.failure_state.by_kind` | Node kind mapped to a replacement template that removes the failure. Use `{noop}` for a statement that can simply be dropped. Leave out kinds for which no replacement is valid in general, such as returning a value. Every entry here must have a matching failure site listed under `kinds.failure_state.nodes`, and every listed failure site that can be rewritten should have an entry here. For an error-propagation construct written as an operator on an operand, a template that keeps the operand through `{child0}` is appropriate only when the result is valid wherever that construct can appear |
| `operators.failure_state.returned_literal_swaps` | Pairs of literals that can replace each other as a returned value: the two boolean literals, and 0 and 1 |
| `operators.state_write` | Always `{"statement": "{noop}"}`: a write that is a statement of its own is replaced by the empty statement |
| `operators.error_order` | Always `{"swap_next": true}` |

## Rules

- Be precise rather than broad: a wrong kind produces changes that do not parse or do not compile. This applies to every node kind, field name, operator token, attribute kind, and prefix string anywhere in the pack.
- Confirm names against the target grammar, not against similar languages, example packs, or the intended meaning of a construct. If a feature has several possible spellings, include only verified spellings; an empty optional list is safer than a guessed entry.
- Keep failure sites actionable: list a failure kind only when the pack can neutralize it, either through a replacement template, a prefix entry for call-shaped failures, or the returned-literal swaps for a returned literal. Do not list a site and then leave it without an operator.
- Cover call-shaped failure signals with the prefix map on the correct call node kind, including ordinary calls, not only macro-like syntax. Reuse the same call node kind that the grammar uses for standalone call statements when the same construct can be a failure signal.
- Include both outer and inner attribute forms for test regions when the language has both, and make the markers match the written attribute text exactly.
- Keep the pack small: at most 40 lines and 2,500 characters, formatted like the examples. Put short arrays on one line, omit optional fields entirely when the format says to leave them out, and add no comments or padding. Count both lines and characters before returning; a pack over either limit is not usable.
- Do not include anything specific to a particular project, library or file.

## Output

Return only the JSON object of the pack, with no text before or after it.

| `string_kinds` | Node kinds of string literals, including multi-part, template, raw, byte, or prefixed forms only when the grammar defines them as separate node kinds. Nothing inside them is ever touched |
| `unwrap_kinds` | Node kinds of a parenthesis wrapper that belongs to a statement's syntax around a condition. When a condition is such a wrapper, the engine works on the expression inside it. Empty when conditions are not wrapped, or when the parentheses are only unnamed tokens rather than a node |
| `test_attribute_markers` | Text fragments of attributes or annotations that mark test-only code inside a production file. | --- | --- |
